newsitem.title: INDIA: India plans second green revolution to boost crops.
newsitem.headline: India plans second green revolution to boost crops.

text.p: India, self-sufficient in foodgrain, is planning a second "green revolution" to cultivate untapped land and boost crop yields, the agriculture minister and officials said on Thursday.

"Practically, what is called a green revolution is only in 30 percent of the area so far under cultivation," Agriculture Minister Chaturanan Mishra told an economic editors conference. "Seventy percent of the area is still untested."

Agriculture ministry officials said only 46 million hectares (113 million acres) had been brought under irrigation, part of the first "green revolution" ushered in the 1960s, out of a total 142 million hectares (350 million acres) available.
Analysts said the green revolution of the 1960s and 1970s had lost its impact in the 1980s and farmers depended more on rains as crop yields stagnated.

India has enjoyed nine consecutive good monsoons. Government expects foodgrain output in 1996/97 (July-June) to reach 197 million tonnes compared with 185 million tonnes in 1995/96, primarily due to good rainfall distribution.
A foodgrain importer until the early 1980s, India in recent years has been exporting rice and wheat with an increase in output.
Mishra said productivity needed to be increased in non-irrigated areas mainly in eastern and northeastern states.
Ministry officials said the new United Front coalition government wanted to usher in a second green revolution by turning green patches into fertile cropland.
"Our effort is to improve multi-crop areas or change cropping systems," K. Rajan, the highest ranking civil servant in the agriculture ministry, told Reuters.
Officials said the first green revolution had focused on mainly rice and wheat crops in northern and southern India.
Mishra said there was stagnation in India's agricultural output with production either rising or dipping by a million tonnes.
"This is dangerous and we have decided to move forward," Mishra said.
Ministry officials said it was impossible to meet the foodgrain production target of 230 million tonnes by the year 2000 unless steps were taken to increase productivity with improved technology.
Agriculture employs about two-thirds of India's work force and accounts for over a third of its gross domestic product.
